Sarita wobbled on the new cycle in the village lane, then fell into the dust for the third time.

Her brother Vishal laughed loudly. "Look, she can't even ride! Baby! Baby!"

Sarita's lip trembled. She threw a pebble at him.

Vishal ran straight to the kitchen. "Amma! Sarita threw a stone at me!"

Amma was frying puris, sweat on her forehead. "Both of you, stop it!"

"But she started—"

"Vishal, you laughed at her. I heard." Amma turned back to the pan, tired.

Vishal went outside. Sarita wasn't speaking to him now. And Amma hadn't taken his side at all.

qa.q: How many times did Sarita fall off the cycle?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: Why did Vishal run to tell Amma?
qa.a: He hoped to win Amma's favour and get Sarita in trouble, after mocking her for falling.

qa.q: What went wrong for Vishal, and what could he try instead?
qa.a: Mocking and tattling left Amma tired and Sarita angry; he could help Sarita learn to ride instead.

qa.q: How does Sarita feel after being laughed at?
qa.a: She feels hurt and humiliated, then angry enough to throw a pebble and stop speaking to Vishal.

grounding: Vishal mocks his sister's failure and runs to tell on her to win his mother's favour, but both lose as Amma is tired and Sarita now has a real grievance.

In their flat in Izmir, Zeynep's brother Emir got a low mark on his spelling test and hid the paper under his bed.

Zeynep found it. She waved it in the air. "Emir got four out of twenty! Four!"

Emir went red. "Give it back!"

She didn't. She ran to their mother, who was paying bills at the table. "Anne, Emir hid his test!"

Their mother sighed and rubbed her eyes. "Zeynep, why are you telling me this now?"

Emir stood in the doorway, glaring at his sister. Later, he took her favourite pen and wouldn't give it back.

Now they were both in trouble, and their mother was even more tired.

qa.q: What mark did Emir get on his spelling test?
qa.a: Four out of twenty.

qa.a: She hoped to win her mother's approval and make Emir look bad.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Zeynep have done instead?
qa.a: Tattling made their mother more tired and gave Emir a real grievance; Zeynep could have kept quiet or encouraged Emir to tell himself.

qa.q: How does Emir feel after his sister waves his test around?
qa.a: He feels humiliated and angry, and takes revenge by keeping her favourite pen.

grounding: Zeynep mocks her brother's low mark and tells on him to gain favour, but it tires their mother and gives Emir a real grievance.

Varun's ears went pink.

At lunch Varun marched to the staffroom. "Sir, Hemant was laughing at me and saying bad words!"

Hemant hadn't said any bad words. Mr Joshi, busy marking forty notebooks, called both brothers in.

"Hemant, did you laugh at him?"

"...Yes."

"Varun, did he say bad words?"

"...No."

Mr Joshi rubbed his forehead. "Both of you, sit here till the bell."

Neither of them got what he wanted.

qa.a: In the first over of the house cricket match, for a duck.

Manjula, you're sulking because your cousins won't let you play their card game? Your Neelam dadi knows exactly how that feels.

I was the youngest of four. My sisters and brother always had games I wasn't allowed in. "You're too small." "You don't know the rules." When they did let me play, I was always the thief, never the police.

I used to shout, "It's not fair!" and they'd laugh, which made it worse. I didn't want to be tolerated. I wanted them to look at me like I mattered.

The turning point came one summer when my eldest sister, Kamla, broke her arm. She couldn't play, so she taught me the rules properly, all of them. The next day, I beat my brother.

He never called me small again.

qa.q: How many siblings did Neelam have?
qa.a: Three; she was the youngest of four.

qa.q: What did young Neelam really want from her older siblings?
qa.a: She wanted to be taken seriously and looked up to, not just tolerated, and felt left out and hurt.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Neelam dadi's story?
qa.a: When Kamla, with a broken arm, taught her the rules properly, and she beat her brother the next day.

qa.q: How might Kamla have felt teaching her youngest sister?
qa.a: She may have felt bored and restless with a broken arm, and then pleased and proud when Neelam won.

grounding: Neelam dadi recalls being the bossed, left-out youngest who wanted to be taken seriously, and the turning point when a sister taught her properly.

Noor stood half in the rain, watching. When she shouted out an answer, Arif said, "That doesn't count. You're not playing."

"That's not fair!"

"Life's not fair," said Hiba, and they both laughed.

Noor kicked a puddle. She didn't want them to be nice to her. She wanted them to think she was good at something.

Reena was the youngest in their house in Jaipur, and her older brothers, Sonu and Yogi, had a secret club in the storeroom. A sign on the door said NO GIRLS, NO BABIES.

"I'm not a baby!" Reena shouted through the door.

"You're seven!" Sonu shouted back.

She sat outside, arms folded. When they came out, she asked, "Can I carry the torch next time?"

"Maybe," said Yogi, which meant no.

At dinner she complained to Papa. "They never let me in! It's not fair!"

Papa said, "Boys, let her in sometimes."

"Fine," Sonu sighed. "She can sit in the corner."

Reena didn't want to sit in the corner. She wanted to be the one holding the torch.

The power had gone during exam week, and both boys were studying by candlelight at the dining table, Darshan for Class 7 maths, Zubin for Class 4 English.

Their mother used to say, "Look at Darshan, he never needs help." Not anymore. She had stopped comparing them after Zubin cried himself to sleep one night.

Now she looked at each of their notebooks separately. "Darshan, you worked out that long sum on your own. That took patience." Then, "Zubin, you rewrote that answer three times until it was neat. I noticed."

Later the boys argued over the last candle. Mummy stayed in the kitchen. They sorted it out: one candle, both sides of the table.

Neither of them needed to be better than the other that night.

qa.q: How did the boys study during the power cut?
qa.a: By candlelight at the dining table.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel when his mother praised his neat answer?
qa.a: He probably felt proud and noticed for his own effort, without being compared to Darshan.

qa.q: Why was staying in the kitchen during the candle argument a good choice?
qa.a: It let the boys solve a small quarrel themselves, since it wasn't a safety issue, and they found a fair answer.

qa.q: How might Darshan see his mother's new way of praising?
qa.a: He may feel valued for his own patience, and less pressure to always be the one who never needs help.

grounding: During a power cut, the mother praises each son's own effort instead of comparing them and lets them solve a small quarrel, so they have less need to beat each other.

For years Indu had said, "Why can't you be like your sister?" to Baljeet, and "Look how fast Baljeet runs" to Simran. The fights in their Amritsar home got worse every year.

So she changed. When Simran brought home a drawing, Indu said, "You used so many colours. You must have thought hard about that." When Baljeet came back from football, she said, "You kept trying even after the first goal went in."

When they argued over the TV remote, she stayed in the kitchen, only calling, "Sort it out yourselves, please."

After a month, she noticed something. They argued less. Yesterday, Baljeet even told Simran, "Your drawing's nice." Simran looked so surprised she dropped her crayons.

Nana sat on the bench at the colony park in Lucknow, watching Neelam and her brother Kiku. They had fought all morning over the swing.

Then Thomas, a big boy from the next building, pushed Kiku off the slide. "Move, shorty."

Before Nana could get up, Neelam was there. She stood in front of Kiku, hands on hips. "Don't push my brother."

Thomas laughed. Kiku stood up beside her. "Yeah. Don't push my sister either."

Thomas shrugged and wandered off.

Nana watched them walk back to the swing, arguing again about whose turn it was. He smiled. The same two who fought at home had stood shoulder to shoulder in thirty seconds.

qa.q: What did Thomas say when he pushed Kiku?
qa.a: "Move, shorty."

qa.q: How does Nana feel watching Neelam and Kiku stand together?
qa.a: He feels warm and amused, smiling at how quickly they defended each other despite their fighting.

qa.q: What could Nana say to the children later?
qa.a: He could tell them he noticed how they stood up for each other, so they see the loyalty behind their fights.

qa.q: How might Kiku feel when Neelam steps in front of him?
qa.a: He probably feels protected and proud of his sister, and brave enough to stand beside her.

grounding: Nana notices his grandchildren, who fight constantly, defending each other against an outsider, showing rivalry and loyalty living together.

I'm Urmila, Jasleen and Gurnoor's Nani, and I've spent every summer watching those two fight. Over the window seat, the last mango, the remote. You name it.

But last week at the park, something happened. A group of older girls started laughing at Gurnoor's thick glasses. I was about to get up.

Jasleen got there first. She walked straight up to them and said, "That's my sister. Leave her alone." Then she took Gurnoor's hand and walked her away.
